title: Norfolk Southern Railway v. State Corporation Commission
description: Whether Code § 56-16.3, which allows private broadband service providers to install fiber optic cables across railroad property, constitutes an unconstitutional taking of private property for a nonpublic use under Article I, Section 11 of the Virginia Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Norfolk Southern argued that Code § 56-16.3, as applied to allow a private, for-profit company like Cox to take its property for financial gain, violates the Virginia Constitution's prohibition against taking private property for nonpublic use and improperly shifts the burden of proving public use.
defendant_argument: The State Corporation Commission implicitly argued that Code § 56-16.3 was constitutional and that the proposed crossings did not impose an "undue hardship" on Norfolk Southern, thereby allowing the taking for broadband expansion.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the State Corporation Commission, ruling that Code § 56-16.3, as applied, unconstitutionally permits a private broadband service provider to take railroad property for a nonpublic use.

title: Layla H v. Virginia
description: Whether the Commonwealth of Virginia's fossil fuel permitting policies and related statutes violate the constitutional and public trust rights of youth plaintiffs, or if these claims are barred by sovereign immunity and lack of standing.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Commonwealth's policies and statutes contribute to climate change, infringing on their jus publicum rights and constitutional rights to life, liberty, property, personal security, and bodily integrity. They contended that sovereign immunity does not bar claims under self-executing constitutional provisions (Article I, § 11) or jus publicum.
defendant_argument: The Commonwealth argued that sovereign immunity bars all claims, that the plaintiffs lacked standing because their alleged injuries were not justiciable, that the relief sought would not redress their injuries, and that the alleged injuries were not caused by the defendants. They also asserted that Article I, § 11 does not contain a substantive due process component and Virginia does not recognize the unenumerated environmental rights.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the Circuit Court of the City of Richmond, dismissing the plaintiffs' complaint with prejudice, finding that the plaintiffs lacked standing to bring the suit.

title: Vlaming v. West Point School Board
description: Whether a public school teacher's refusal to use a transgender student's preferred pronouns, based on religious beliefs, constitutes a protected exercise of religious freedom and free speech, or if the school board can compel such speech as part of employment duties.
plaintiff_argument: Vlaming claims he lost his job not because of something he had said, but because his conscience would not allow him to use government-mandated pronouns, which he believes violates his sincerely held religious beliefs and free speech rights.
defendant_argument: The School Board terminated Vlaming for refusing to use masculine pronouns and comply with directives, arguing his actions violated policies prohibiting harassment and discrimination based on gender identity, and that his speech was part of his official duties.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed the circuit court's dismissal of Vlaming's free exercise, free speech, due process, and breach of contract claims, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: McKeithen v. City of Richmond
description: Whether Code § 58.1-3967, which directs unclaimed surplus proceeds from a tax sale to the City after its tax lien is satisfied, unconstitutionally infringes upon the property rights of a partially satisfied junior lienor.
plaintiff_argument: The Caldwell Trust argued that the circuit court's interpretation of Code § 58.1-3967, as applied, violates the Virginia Constitution by taking its property interest in the surplus proceeds and transferring it to the City, even though the City's tax lien was fully satisfied and the Caldwell Trust's lien was not.
defendant_argument: The City argued that the $14,000 unclaimed portion of the surplus proceeds escheats to the City under Code § 58.1-3967, even though its tax lien had been fully satisfied, and that the Caldwell Trust did not have a property interest in those specific funds.
decision_outcome: The court held that the escheat provision of Code § 58.1-3967, as applied to this case, violates Article I, Section 11 of the Constitution of Virginia by unconstitutionally infringing upon property rights, and reversed the circuit court's ruling.

title: Anderson v. Clarke
description: Whether Antoine Anderson is entitled to enhanced earned sentence credits retroactively under HB 5148, or if Item 404(R)(2) of the 2022 Appropriation Act limits his earned sentence credits to the lower rate.
plaintiff_argument: Anderson argued that VDOC misapplied Item 404(R)(2), which should only apply prospectively, and that he should receive enhanced ESCs retroactively under HB 5148 for time served before July 1, 2022. He also argued VDOC's interpretation violated ex post facto and due process clauses.
defendant_argument: VDOC argued that it correctly applied the statutory ESC scheme as modified by Item 404(R)(2), which caps Anderson's ESCs at 4.5 per 30 days due to his disqualifying offense, and that this interpretation did not violate any constitutional rights.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, denying Anderson's petition for a writ of habeas corpus.

title: Taylor v. Northam
description: Whether an 1890 deed and an 1889 joint resolution prohibit the Governor of Virginia from ordering the removal of a state-owned monument from state-owned property.
plaintiff_argument: The Taylor Plaintiffs contend that Governor Northam has no authority to remove the Lee Monument because the 1889 Joint Resolution binds him to perpetually maintain it, violating the Virginia Constitution and property rights established by the 1887 and 1890 Deeds, and that the 2020 Budget Amendment is unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: Governor Northam argues he has the authority to remove the monument, that the language in the deeds is merely precatory and does not create enforceable restrictive covenants, and that enforcing such covenants would violate public policy and be unreasonable due to changed circumstances, with the 2020 Budget Amendment supporting the removal.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed the circuit court's judgment, concluding that the purported restrictive covenants are unenforceable, Governor Northam's order did not violate the Constitution, and all of the Taylor Plaintiffs' claims are without merit.
